query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: A carefully controlled annealing treatment that induces the formation of nanoscale, coherent precipitates within the fcc FeCoNi matrix will increase magnetic coercivity by creating local strain fields and enhanced magnetic anisotropy that promote domain wall pinning.
generation.material_initial_state: An almost equiatomic fcc FeCoNi high-entropy alloy exhibiting high saturation magnetization but low coercivity.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to a controlled annealing process at temperatures high enough to mobilize limited diffusion yet below the order–disorder transition temperature, to induce the precipitation of a secondary phase while retaining the high-entropy equiatomic composition.
generation.conditions: The treatment should be applied under conditions that preserve the overall single-phase fcc structure and maintain the configurational entropy of at least 1.0R, with the annealing temperature and duration optimized to produce uniformly distributed nanoscale, coherent precipitates.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale, coherent precipitates that form within the fcc matrix.
generation.mechanism: The precipitates introduce local strain and modify the magnetic anisotropy at the particle interfaces, effectively acting as pinning centers for magnetic domain walls. This enhanced domain-wall pinning mechanism is expected to increase the coercivity compared to a homogeneous FeCoNi alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable increase in coercivity (predicted to be greater than 20% relative to the as-cast or quenched FeCoNi baseline) while maintaining high saturation magnetization.
generation.baseline: The conventional, rapidly cooled (as-cast or quenched) FeCoNi alloy without the induced nanoscale precipitate structure.
generation.boundary: This outcome is expected only when the alloy composition remains nearly equiatomic and the fcc phase is preserved, ensuring high configurational entropy; deviations from these parameters may not yield the desired increase in coercivity.
generation.uncertainty: The exact percentage increase in coercivity is uncertain and may depend on precise annealing conditions; however, a significant increase (e.g., greater than 20%) is anticipated if the microstructural intervention is successful.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nearly equiatomic fcc FeCoNi samples: one set as a control (rapidly cooled to retain a homogeneous fcc structure) and another set subjected to the controlled annealing treatment designed to induce the formation of nanoscale, coherent precipitates. Characterize the microstructure using TEM or similar high-resolution imaging to confirm precipitate formation and perform magnetic hysteresis loop measurements at room temperature.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM imaging of precipitate distribution and size)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a coercivity increase of greater than 20% relative to the control samples, or if precipitates are not observed despite the annealing treatment, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Polymorphism, which describes the occurrence of different lattice structures in a crystalline material, is a critical phenomenon in materials science and condensed matter physics. Recently, configuration disorder was compositionally engineered into single lattices, leading to the discovery of high-entropy alloys and high-entropy oxides. For these novel entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter with extremely high structural stability, is polymorphism still possible? Here by employing in situ high-pressure synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction, we reveal a polymorphic transition from face-centred-cubic ( fcc ) structure to hexagonal-close-packing ( hcp ) structure in the prototype CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy. The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures. As pressure is increased, the critical temperature for the hcp -to- fcc transformation also rises.

The CoCrFeMnNi HEA sample was synthesized using a gas-atomization technique [34] . The gas-atomized powders are spherical particles with a typical size ranging from a few microns to tens of microns, which are appropriate for high-pressure experiments ( Supplementary Fig. 1 ). These particles are polycrystalline with a grain size ranging from submicron to a few microns (the inset of Supplementary Fig. 1 ). The chemical and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy analyses confirm that the composition of the as-atomized CoCrFeMnNi HEA is close to the nominal composition, and there are no compositional changes after the high-pressure XRD tests ( Supplementary Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 1 ).

The structural stability of the prototype CoCrFeMnNi HEA has been extensively studied in a wide temperature range from 55 K to its melting temperature of ∼1,600 K at ambient pressure [19] [31] [37] [38] but to our knowledge, no polymorphic transition has been observed. Conversely, high-pressure studies remain a virgin area in HEAs. In this work, using in situ high-pressure XRD techniques, we observed the first polymorphic transition from fcc to hcp in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA, as shown in Fig. 1c . Therefore, some critical questions are how and why can an hcp HEA form at high-pressure and can it be maintained at ambient conditions? According to the d -spacing of the main reflections of both fcc and hcp (that is, (111) and (220) of fcc , and (100), (002), (101) and (110) of hcp , as a function of pressure shown in Fig. 2a ), it is clear that the hcp -(002) and hcp -(110) planes inherit the fcc -(111) and fcc -(220) planes, respectively. In addition, Fig. 2b shows no obvious volume collapse during the transition; both the fcc and hcp phases seem to have almost the same volume per atom and bulk modulus. frame.system: An fcc FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy whose baseline is an almost equiatomic FeCoNi system that exhibits high saturation magnetization but low intrinsic coercivity.
frame.goal: To achieve a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with noticeably higher coercivity than the previously studied soft ferromagnetic derivatives (FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt) while maintaining an equiatomic multicomponent composition and a configurational entropy of at least 1.0R.
frame.limitation: Prior derivatives (FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt) have shown soft ferromagnetism with low coercive fields, meaning that although the magnetic saturation is high, domain wall pinning or anisotropy is insufficient to increase coercivity.

decision.trend: Earlier high‐entropy alloy studies focusing on FeCoNi‐based systems (via additions such as Pd and Pt) maintained high saturation magnetization but did not tackle the intrinsic soft ferromagnetism issue because they did not introduce features (e.g., microstructural inhomogeneity) that promote domain‐wall pinning. In parallel, several HEA studies have successfully employed thermal treatments to induce nanoscale precipitates or ordered regions (even in fcc matrices) to modify mechanical properties through controlled phase architecture. Thus, there is a trend moving from mere compositional modifications (which in these magnetic systems lead to soft behavior) towards using processing routes that engineer a tailored microstructure with secondary phases to achieve additional functionalities.
decision.unsolved: How to boost coercivity in an equiatomic fcc FeCoNi alloy while preserving high saturation magnetization and the requisite high configurational entropy remains unsolved. Specifically, the challenge is to generate intrinsic magnetic anisotropy or pinning centers without resorting to non-equiatomic or low-entropy modifications.
decision.lever: Apply a carefully controlled thermal treatment (annealing) to induce the controlled precipitation of a nanoscale, coherent, second phase within the fcc FeCoNi matrix
decision.why: This intervention builds on the trend of moving toward microstructural engineering in HEAs. By inducing fine, coherent precipitates through thermal processing (at temperatures below the order–disorder transition yet high enough to mobilize limited diffusion), local magnetic hardening (via enhanced domain-wall pinning from interfacial strain and increased magnetic anisotropy) can be achieved. This lever directly addresses the soft ferromagnetism observed in prior Pd- and Pt-bearing derivatives and provides a discriminating test: if the heat-treated alloy shows a marked (e.g., >20%) increase in coercivity (measured via hysteresis loop analysis) relative to a baseline cast/quench FeCoNi alloy, the hypothesis is supported; if not, the approach is falsified.
